rows.grounds: vocative-like epithet in compound sense; cit-nātha
demonstrative pronoun, sandhi form of asau

items.question: How does the lord of consciousness manifest time?
premises: Past and future dissolve into the present moment.
The present itself also dissolves in consciousness.
The lord of consciousness is the agent who manifests time.
items.inference: Because past, future, and present all dissolve in consciousness, time is fully manifested by the lord of consciousness alone.
items.plain_english: Therefore, through the dissolution of past and future, and also through the dissolution of the present, this god, the lord of consciousness himself, fully makes time manifest.

items.question: What is the nature of transmigration for consciousness that manifests time?
premises: The lord of consciousness manifests time as its own appearance.
Transmigration arises within that same consciousness.
Transmigration contains the manifestation of consciousness's own nature.
items.inference: For consciousness whose nature manifests time, transmigration is the play of being and nonbeing appearing within its own form.
items.plain_english: Thus, for this consciousness whose nature is to manifest time, transmigration—containing the manifestation of its own nature—appears among beings as consisting of being and nonbeing within its own form.

rows.grounds: passive verb, sandhi form of abhidhīyate
relative pronoun, sandhi form of yat

items.question: How is the unfolding of knowerhood described in its own form?
premises: Abiding in its own form is the unfolding of knowerhood.
Knowerhood involves the distinction between 'I' and 'this'.
It also involves negations such as 'not this' and further determinations like 'that'.
items.inference: The unfolding of knowerhood is the dynamic abiding in one's own form through affirmations and negations of 'I', 'this', and 'that'.
items.plain_english: Abiding in its own form is called the unfolding of knowerhood: 'this is not what I am', and 'I am what is not this', and also 'this is that'.

rows.grounds: relative pronoun, sandhi form of yat

items.question: What is the status of pure knowerhood in relation to the manifestation of nonbeing?
premises: The cognition 'this is not this' is a varied manifestation of nonbeing.
Supreme knowerhood is pure in itself.
In pure knowerhood there is no separate abiding of such distinctions.
items.inference: The varied play of nonbeing belongs to manifestation, but pure knowerhood itself does not contain separate abiding of those distinctions.
items.plain_english: The varied cognition expressed as 'this is not this' is the supreme appearing of nonbeing; but in that pure knowerhood there is no separate abiding of such distinctions.

rows.grounds: relative pronoun, sandhi form of yaḥ

items.question: Why is isolated pure knowerhood insufficient to explain worldly cognition?
premises: In the purely isolated aspect of knowerhood there is no cognition as such.
Worldly knowerhood always involves determinate cognition.
Worldly knowerhood is therefore of a different, differentiated kind.
items.inference: Pure isolated knowerhood cannot account for cognition, whereas all worldly knowerhood is constituted by such differentiated cognition.
items.plain_english: In that isolated aspect there is no cognition at all, so what use is that isolated state? But every worldly state of being a knower is of this differentiated kind.

items.question: What makes the cognition of nonbeing possible?
premises: Nonbeing can appear as an object of cognition.
Such appearance depends on the operation of time.
The absolute consciousness is perfectly full and contains all forms.
items.inference: The cognition of nonbeing is possible because the perfectly full consciousness, through time, manifests even absence within itself.
items.plain_english: There, nonbeing becomes an object of cognition, and that happens through the grace of time; for this perfectly full reality bears the form of all things and the self of all.

rows.grounds: object of knowing, sandhi form of meyaḥ
optative/imperative sense in rhetorical question, sandhi form of avatiṣṭhatām

items.question: Can knower, knowing, and known stand as independently real entities?
premises: Knower, cognition, and known are mutually defined roles.
If they were absolutely real, their status would not be relative.
Their actual functioning depends on mutual relation.
items.inference: Knower, cognition, and known cannot stand as independently real entities because their status is inherently relative.
items.plain_english: Where could the knower stand, where cognition, and where the known object? For if knower and the rest were absolutely real, their status could not be merely relative.

items.question: Why can the knower not be established independently of the known?
premises: The being of the knower is conceived only in relation to the known.
If their mutual form is absent, the relation cannot be established.
If their mutual form is present, independence is still impossible because of incompatibility.
items.inference: The knower cannot be established independently, since its being depends on the known in every case.
items.plain_english: The being of the knower and the rest is conceived only from the known; whether their mutual form is absent or present, it cannot stand independently because of their incompatibility.

items.question: What further problems arise if knower and known are taken as independently real?
premises: Independent reality would lead to overextension everywhere.
It would wrongly entail omniscience and similar properties.
Noncontributing factors do not manifest simultaneously as required.
items.inference: Treating knower and known as independently real creates logical overreach and impossible consequences.
items.plain_english: This view fails because it would lead to overextension everywhere, would entail omniscience and the like, and because noncontributing factors do not manifest all at once.

rows.grounds: compound anutpanna-samatva + eva with sandhi, instrumental

items.question: Why does deriving knowerhood from another object fail to explain it?
premises: Knowerhood might be thought to arise from another known object.
That explanation would require yet another source for that state.
The resulting state would remain equivalent to something unarisen.
items.inference: Explaining knowerhood through another known object leads to regress and leaves knowerhood effectively unestablished.
items.plain_english: If knowerhood were produced by some other known object, then its own arising would depend on something else again, and so it would remain as if unarisen.

items.question: How does the full consciousness give rise to the division of I and this?
premises: The ultimate reality is full consciousness, Shiva.
That consciousness can differentiate its own aspects.
The division into 'not I' and 'this' arises within that differentiation.
items.inference: The division between subject and object is a constructed differentiation within the one full consciousness.
items.plain_english: Therefore this full consciousness, Shiva, dividing its own aspect, constructs the differentiated part beginning with 'not I' and also the object 'this'.

rows.grounds: quotation marker, sandhi form of iti

items.question: How do the senses of I and not-I arise within the self?
premises: The self contains the fullness of all that is other than any limited part.
The sense 'I' arises by appropriating that fullness to itself.
The sense 'not I' arises by withdrawing fullness from what is taken as other.
items.inference: The experiences of 'I' and 'not I' are complementary movements of appropriation and withdrawal within the one self.
items.plain_english: The 'I' takes to itself, to that extent, the fullness of everything other; and from what is other there also arises the withdrawing sense of 'not I'.

items.question: How do the I-part and this-part relate to each other in cognition?
premises: The I-part and the this-part arise together in cognition.
Each part excludes the other in its own functioning.
The I-part can conceal the this-part within its own domain.
items.inference: The I and this aspects of experience are mutually exclusive yet dynamically related within the same cognition.
items.plain_english: These two parts mutually exclude each other; the own 'I' conceals the 'this' part, which stands in cognition, within its own 'I'-aspect.

items.question: Does concealment in cognition destroy the concealed object?
premises: The I-aspect can conceal the this-aspect in cognition.
Concealment does not dissolve or annihilate what is concealed.
The concealed object remains established in cognition, though bound by convention.
items.inference: Cognitive concealment is like covering, not destruction; the concealed remains present within cognition.
items.plain_english: It remains and does not dissolve it, just like a pot covered by a cloth; that same thing, though tied by convention, remains established in cognition.

rows.grounds: compound aham-aṃśa-vyapohin, genitive/ablative sense in context

items.question: How do the I and this arise through mutual exclusion?
premises: The sense of 'this' arises through inner contraction that excludes the I-part.
The sense of 'I' arises through exclusion of the mass of thisness.
Both arise from within the same consciousness.
items.inference: The poles of 'I' and 'this' are formed by reciprocal exclusion within one inner field of consciousness.
items.plain_english: The 'this' arises from inner contraction that excludes the 'I'-part, and the 'I' arises from within through exclusion of the whole mass of 'thisness'.

items.question: What underlies the manifestation of successive exclusions of I and other?
premises: Experience involves exclusion of one's own I and of other I-senses.
These exclusions manifest in patterned forms.
They proceed by depending on six deities characterized as empty forms.
items.inference: The play of mutual exclusions operates through six empty-form deities that structure manifestation.
uncertainties: The precise identity of the six deities is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: From the exclusion of one's own 'I' and the exclusion of other and other 'I'-senses there arises manifestation; relying on which, the six deities of empty form proceed.

rows.grounds: predicate noun, sandhi form of vikalpaḥ

items.question: How are conceptual construction and time related in manifestation?
premises: The cognition 'that is indeed this' is called conceptual construction.
Time is that by which the universe is articulated.
The universe is articulated through the arising of its own limited parts.
items.inference: Conceptual construction and time are the same differentiating power by which the universe appears as articulated parts.
items.plain_english: The cognition 'that is indeed this' is called conceptual construction; and that is time, by which the universe is articulated through the arising of its own parts.

rows.grounds: relative pronoun, sandhi form of yaḥ

items.question: What is the luminous aspect present within differentiated manifestation?
premises: Within the differentiated part there is an aspect of manifestation.
That aspect is self-luminous.
As the form of being, it animates all appearances.
items.inference: Even within differentiation there remains a self-luminous aspect whose nature is to animate all manifestation.
items.plain_english: In that part there is this aspect of manifestation, self-luminous in the form of being; that is the very nature which animates all things.

rows.grounds: relative pronoun, sandhi form of yaḥ
contrastive particle, sandhi form of tu

items.question: How is the aspect of nonbeing characterized in relation to knower, knowing, and known?
premises: The luminous aspect is not defined as knower, cognition, or known.
There is also an aspect connected with emptiness.
That aspect appears as nonbeing and is associated with Rudra.
items.inference: Beyond the triad of knower, knowing, and known, manifestation includes an emptiness-aspect of nonbeing associated with Rudra.
items.plain_english: That is not defined as knower, nor as cognition, nor as known; but that aspect which, through connection with emptiness, appears as nonbeing has Rudra as its deity.

rows.grounds: compound mātṛtā-abhimukha/abhivata sense; read as mātṛtā-abhivataḥ
quotation marker, sandhi form of iti

items.question: How does nonbeing become cognition and give rise to the triad?
premises: The emptiness-aspect associated with Rudra can become cognition.
Through its connection, knowerhood is oriented and articulated.
From cognition the known becomes distinguished as separate.
items.inference: The same underlying aspect becomes cognition and thereby unfolds into knower, knowing, and known.
uncertainties: The compound mātṛtābhāvivataḥ is morphologically compressed; analysis follows the transmitted fused form.
items.plain_english: That very aspect becomes cognition; through its connection knowerhood is oriented, and from cognition the known stands apart. Thus it has been established.

rows.grounds: instrumental plural, sandhi form of kaiḥ

items.question: Who understood time in this way as a mode of cognition?
premises: The preceding verses established time as a mode of cognition.
This understanding was received within a specific teaching lineage.
The lineage is identified by devotion to the guru called Bhavatī.
items.inference: The doctrine that time is a mode of cognition was understood by those who served the revered guru known as Bhavatī.
uncertainties: The exact identity of the guru called Bhavatī is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: In this way, the status of time as cognition was understood here by certain teachers who attended upon the revered guru feet known as Bhavatī.

items.question: What is the group of six sheaths said to do in the individual self?
premises: The individual self shines with the joy of consciousness's nature.
A group of six factors is declared in that context.
These six are called the sheaths and are associated with giving knowerhood.
items.inference: The six sheaths are the limiting factors that confer finite knowerhood upon the individual self.
items.plain_english: Thus, in the individual self—shining with the joy of the glory of consciousness's nature and receiving knowerhood—there is declared the group of six called the sheaths.

rows.grounds: contrastive particle, sandhi form of tu

items.question: How do different thinkers explain the cognitive role of the six sheaths?
premises: The six sheaths are associated with cognition.
Some thinkers assign cognitive status to each sheath individually.
Others hold that one sheath functions with the assistance of all the others.
items.inference: There are divergent views on whether cognition belongs to each sheath separately or to one sheath aided by the rest.
items.plain_english: Some have accepted that each one of them has the status of cognition, but others think that one of them functions with all the others as its assistants.

items.question: What further opinions exist about how the sheaths operate in cognition?
premises: Thinkers disagree about the cognitive role of the six sheaths.
Some propose occasional or situational operation of particular sheaths.
Others propose operation by pairs or by combinations of triads and pairs.
items.inference: The sheaths are variously explained as operating situationally, in pairs, or in mixed combinations.
items.plain_english: Others say that sometimes, somehow, somewhere, some one of them operates, and so on; others hold that they operate in pairs, and others by combinations of a triad and a pair.
